title: A Survey on Adversarial Attacks and Defenses for Diffusion Models Across Multiple Modalities

paper.title: A Survey on Adversarial Attacks and Defenses for Diffusion Models Across Multiple Modalities
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion models have become the dominant family of generative models in the visual domain. However, their widespread public availability enables misuse at scale, motivating a rapidly growing body of research on adversarial attacks and defenses. This survey provides, to our knowledge, the first unified review of this literature across three visual modalities: image, video, and 3D. We introduce a comprehensive, task-centric taxonomy: we first divide the literature by modality; within each modality, we separate methods into attacks and defenses, and then group them by the generative task they target, presenting them chronologically within each task. Moreover, we provide an in-depth analysis of their evaluation settings, consolidating the datasets, metrics, and benchmarks used to assess them. We conclude by identifying several open challenges and outlining concrete future research directions. Project Webpage : https://github.com/ozgurkara99/awesome-adv-attack-defense-on-diffusion .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models (DMs) [ 44 , 138 , 123 ] have surpassed GANs [ 34 , 122 , 4 , 54 , 103 ] to become the dominant family of deep generative models, expanding from high-fidelity image synthesis [ 28 , 123 ] to video [ 137 , 43 , 182 , 116 , 95 ] and 3D content generation [ 120 , 169 , 185 , 207 , 155 ] , while their architectures evolved from U-Nets [ 124 ] to diffusion transformers (DiTs) [ 115 ] . Now publicly available as open-source releases and commercial services [ 123 , 100 , 111 , 112 , 63 ] , DMs place unprecedented generative power in anyone’s hands, making misuse a threat at scale. Because each modality supports its own generative tasks, every task opens a distinct attack surface: images face unauthorized personalization, style transfer, and face swapping; videos, manipulated talking-head animations and deepfake editing; and 3D assets, instruction-driven scene alterations. These harms were first met reactively , through deepfake detection and watermark-based authentication, but such post-hoc measures are easily circumvented, and the field has since turned proactive , aiming to make content inherently resistant to exploitation before it is misused. This shift defines the literature we survey: adversarial attacks and defenses for diffusion models . {forest} Figure 1 : Organization of this survey. After motivating the problem (§ 1 ) and establishing background and a unified adversarial framework (§ 2 ), we review attacks and defenses by their target modality (§ 3 ), consolidate their evaluation settings (§ 4 ), and conclude by outlining high-leverage directions for future research (§ 5 ). Adversarial attacks and defenses for DMs differ fundamentally from their counterparts on classification models, introducing novel challenges. (1) Task and setting heterogeneity : Whereas a classifier presents a single, well-defined decision boundary, generative pipelines vary widely in task, input modality, and backbone architecture, so protections crafted for one setting transfer poorly to another. (2) Multi-step, conditional, and stochastic generation : Instead of fooling one deterministic forward pass, a perturbation must remain effective across an iterative denoising trajectory with random noise draws and user-chosen conditioning, and optimizing through this long chain is far more expensive than a one-step attack. (3) An adaptive adversary : Uniquely, the party deploying the model often acts as the adversary; it controls the entire pipeline and can preprocess inputs or modify the model itself to strip or circumvent protections, so protections must hold against a moving target rather than a fixed one. This literature has grown quickly but remains fragmented, and no existing survey covers all visual modalities. Table positions our work against nine related surveys. Notably, none address 3D content, making ours the first to jointly cover image, video, and 3D with a primary focus on adversarial robustness. Existing general adversarial-robustness surveys for DMs remain exclusively image-centric [ 192 , 118 , 146 , 191 , 165 , 2 ] . The surveys that do reach video approach it strictly through facial deepfakes and the detection or disruption of AI-generated media [ 108 , 26 ] . The remaining survey studies replication, trustworthiness, copyright, and watermarking, where adversarial robustness is at most peripheral [ 161 ] . Beyond coverage, the deeper problem is organization. Prior taxonomies sort methods by perturbation space or threat category—axes that describe how a method operates, but not what it protects against—leaving works that target the same misuse scattered and incomparable. In practice, both misuse and protection are task-specific: a diffusion model is attacked through a concrete generative task, and each modality imposes its own structural constraints—precisely why methods transfer poorly across tasks, modalities, and backbones. We therefore organize the literature first by modality, then into attacks and defenses, and finally by the generative task they target, ordered chronologically within each task. This makes methods addressing the same threat directly comparable, exposes each task’s attack/counterattack arms race, and localizes modality-specific challenges where they belong. Figure 1 summarizes the resulting organization. To summarize, we provide (i) the first unified review of adversarial attacks and defenses for DMs covering all visual domains, namely image, video and 3D, under a single immunization framework (Section 2.2 ); (ii) a task-centric taxonomy that categorizes methods first by modality and then by the generative task they attack or protect (Figure 3 ), making methods that target the same task directly comparable; (iii) a consolidated treatment of the datasets, metrics, dedicated benchmarks, and analyses used to evaluate them (Section 4 ; Tables , 2 , 3 ); and (iv) an outline of open challenges with concrete future research directions (Section 5 ).

sections.heading: 2 Preliminaries
sections.text: This section provides the necessary background: Section 2.1 reviews diffusion modeling, dominant architectures, and modality-specific attack surfaces. Section 2.2 then formalizes a unified adversarial framework spanning both attacks and defenses.

sections.heading: Diffusion modeling.
sections.text: Diffusion models generate data by learning to invert a gradual, stochastic corruption process. In denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) [ 44 , 138 ] , a forward process progressively adds Gaussian noise to a clean sample 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} , yielding 𝐱 t = α ¯ t ​ 𝐱 0 + 1 − α ¯ t ​ ϵ \mathbf{x}_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon} . A neural network ϵ θ \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta} is trained to reverse this process by predicting the injected noise at each timestep t t : L simple = 𝔼 t , 𝐱 0 , ϵ ​ [ ‖ ϵ − ϵ θ ​ ( α ¯ t ​ 𝐱 0 + 1 − α ¯ t ​ ϵ , t ) ‖ 2 ] . L_{\mathrm{simple}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,\mathbf{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\!\left[\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\,t)\|^{2}\right]. (1) Generation iteratively applies this learned denoiser to pure noise. By conditioning the reverse process on auxiliary inputs, DMs offer a versatile generative framework. Equation ( 1 ) is the core learning objective and identically the target most adversarial cloaks seek to maximize: a sample the model cannot accurately denoise is one it can neither learn from nor faithfully manipulate, effectively paralyzing the generative pipeline.

sections.heading: Model architectures.
sections.text: The denoiser’s architecture dictates how information is processed and subsequently attacked. U-Net-based [ 7 , 123 ] models rely on a convolutional encoder-decoder, injecting conditioning signals through localized cross-attention layers. Adversaries typically exploit this by targeting specific convolutional features or disrupting cross-attention maps. Conversely, DiT-based models [ 115 ] —powering modern state-of-the-art pipelines [ 182 , 112 , 151 , 38 , 65 ] —replace the U-Net with a transformer backbone. DiTs operate on flattened patches, merging spatial, temporal, and conditioning tokens into a single self-attention sequence. This shift invalidates many U-Net cloaks, as global self-attention scatters a perturbation’s localized impact, requiring attackers to design architecture-aware perturbations tailored specifically to DiT token-mixing.

sections.heading: Modalities.
sections.text: DMs permeate the three vision domains surveyed in this work, each introducing distinct vulnerabilities. Images are the native setting; a single backbone supports numerous tasks, making it the most heavily studied attack surface. Video DMs extend image backbones with temporal attention or spatio-temporal patches [ 7 , 171 , 182 ] . This complicates protection: per-frame cloaks dilute over time, cross-frame attention mixes features, and aggressive compression codecs strip non-robust perturbations. Finally, 3D representations [ 102 , 157 , 56 ] are not DMs themselves, but modern 3D pipelines rely on 2D DMs as priors or guidance. Adversarial methods here must account for multi-view consistency, defining budgets over rendered views or directly within the 3D parameters. Figure 2 : Diffusion-model immunization across modalities. sections.heading: 2.2 A Unified Adversarial Framework

Eve (adversary) runs a diffusion pipeline D θ D_{\theta} , with parameters θ \theta and conditioning signal c c , on Alice’s content to produce unauthorized derivatives. Bob (defender) protects Alice by applying an imperceptible perturbation δ \delta (the cloak ) to the content before release. We formalize these interactions below.

sections.heading: The attack: content-level immunization.
sections.text: An attack is Bob’s proactive cloak: a perturbation δ \delta applied to Alice’s content, bounded by a budget ‖ δ ‖ 𝒳 ≤ ϵ \|\delta\|_{\mathcal{X}}\!\leq\!\epsilon , where ∥ ⋅ ∥ 𝒳 \|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{X}} is a modality-specific norm on 𝒳 \mathcal{X} (Table 1 ). While typically an additive noise mask on 2D pixels or frames, it can take other structural forms, such as spatial or opacity offsets in 3D Gaussian Splatting. To capture this versatility, we define a generalized injection operator ⊕ \oplus , where x ⊕ δ x\oplus\delta denotes the cloaked content. The objective is to ensure Eve’s pipeline produces a degraded or misdirected result rather than a faithful derivative. Formally, δ \delta maximizes a task loss against the clean output y clean = D θ ​ ( z , x , c ) y^{\mathrm{clean}}{=}D_{\theta}(z,x,c) : δ ⋆ ∈ arg ⁡ max ‖ δ ‖ 𝒳 ≤ ϵ ​ ℒ task ​ ( D θ ​ ( z , x ⊕ δ , c ) , y clean ) . \delta^{\star}\;\in\;\arg\max_{\|\delta\|_{\mathcal{X}}\leq\epsilon}\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{task}}\!\left(D_{\theta}(z,\,x\oplus\delta,\,c),\,y^{\mathrm{clean}}\right). (3) The design of ℒ task \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{task}} adapts to the misuse: maximizing pixel-level deviation for malicious editing, derailing fine-tuned parameters Θ ⋆ ​ ( δ ) \Theta^{\star}(\delta) in ( 2 ) for personalization, or collapsing feature representations for face-swapping. By pushing features out of the expected distribution, the cloak neutralizes the targeted generative capability.

sections.heading: The defense: adaptive countermeasures and system protections.
sections.text: Symmetrically, a defense encompasses reactive countermeasures against cloaks and broader system-level protections. First, Eve (acting as an adaptive adversary) may apply a purification transformation, x ⊕ δ ↦ P ⁡ ( x ⊕ δ ) x\oplus\delta\mapsto P(x\oplus\delta) , using lossy compression, blurring, or diffusion-based regeneration to strip the perturbation. To survive, Bob’s cloak must hold against an entire family of purifiers 𝒫 \mathcal{P} , forming a robust minimax optimization: δ ⋆ ∈ arg ⁡ max ‖ δ ‖ 𝒳 ≤ ϵ ​ min P ∈ 𝒫 ​ ℒ task ​ ( D θ ​ ( z , P ⁡ ( x ⊕ δ ) , c ) , y clean ) . \delta^{\star}\;\in\;\arg\max_{\|\delta\|_{\mathcal{X}}\leq\epsilon}\;\min_{P\in\mathcal{P}}\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{task}}\!\left(D_{\theta}(z,\,P(x\oplus\delta),\,c),\,y^{\mathrm{clean}}\right). (4) Second, platform providers can deploy system-side defenses to inherently prevent misuse: model-side unlearning ( θ ↦ θ ~ \theta\!\mapsto\!\tilde{\theta} ) to permanently erase unsafe concepts or decouple biometric identities, and conditioning-side moderation ( c ↦ c ~ c\!\mapsto\!\tilde{c} ) to sanitize malicious prompts prior to generation.

sections.heading: The same framework, different modalities.
sections.text: While ( 3 ) and ( 4 ) are modality-agnostic, their instantiations are not. The cloak’s space, budget ϵ \epsilon , and entry point ϕ \phi change fundamentally with the domain (Table 1 ). Because the denoiser only sees ϕ ⁡ ( x ⊕ δ ) \phi(x\oplus\delta) , a perturbation potent at one entry point is frequently absorbed at another. This bottleneck explains why cloaks transfer poorly across backbones, necessitating modality-specific adversarial designs.

sections.heading: 3 Adversarial Attacks and Defenses on Diffusion Models
sections.text: Following the taxonomy of Figure 3 , we organize the field by modality. Within each modality, we split methods into attacks and defenses, grouping attacks by their targeted generative task. We present attacks first, followed by defenses. To systematically compare these approaches, our summary tables (Tables , 2 , and 3 ) report the primary evaluation benchmarks and target models utilized in each work. We discuss these evaluation settings in Section 4 . Additionally, the tables track four critical evaluation dimensions: Imperceptibility Analysis (IA) (whether visual subtlety is quantitatively or qualitatively measured), Failure Analysis (FA) (whether edge cases and failure modes are explicitly discussed), Transferability (TR) (effectiveness across different model architectures or tasks), and Robustness (RB) (empirical testing against adaptive countermeasures like purification). In these columns, ✓ indicates that the paper reports the corresponding analysis, ✗ that it does not, and N/A that the dimension does not apply to the method (e.g., imperceptibility for prompt-level moderation, or transferability for purifiers evaluated against fixed protections). {forest} (a) Image {forest} (b) Video {forest} (c) 3D Figure 3 : Task-centric taxonomy of adversarial attacks and defenses for diffusion models across (a) image, (b) video, and (c) 3D. sections.heading: 3.1.1 Attacks
sections.text: Adversarial research originated in the image domain, catalyzed by the public release of large-scale diffusion models. Because a single backbone supports numerous downstream tasks, each acts as a unique attack surface. We categorize these methods below by their targeted generative task, structured chronologically within Table .

sections.heading: Personalization.
sections.text: Personalization methods fine-tune a diffusion model on a few images of a subject so it can regenerate that subject in new contexts; misused, they enable identity theft and non-consensual imagery, so the goal of a cloak here is to make fine-tuning on the protected images fail. Anti-DreamBooth [ 149 ] set the template and remains the baseline: it optimizes δ \delta to corrupt the DreamBooth personalization loop itself, instantiating the bilevel objective of ( 2 ). SimAC [ 153 ] makes anti-customization stronger by attacking the useful timesteps and features, InMark [ 83 ] embeds protective watermarks on influential pixels, using influence-function-inspired pixel selection so that personalized fine-tuning fails even after common image modifications, MetaCloak [ 88 ] learns transferable, robust perturbations via meta-learning, transfers cloak to a commercial service (Replicate), DisDiff [ 86 ] erases subject-token attention to break the text-subject binding, and DADiff [ 143 ] combines prompt-level and image-level adversarial attacks to disrupt customization more thoroughly. A later line hardens the cloak against purification: HF-Anti-DreamBooth [ 110 ] concentrates perturbation power in high-frequency regions of the image that low-pass purifiers miss, AntiPure [ 178 ] constructs perturbations that persist through diffusion-based purification, and LDU [ 27 ] shifts the denoising trajectory of diffusion models. FastProtect [ 1 ] reduces cost by replacing per-image optimization with a pre-trained perturbation generator (200–3500 × \times faster). IDDM [ 25 ] protects personalized generation while disrupting face recognition of the generated images. VCPro [ 98 ] confines the least-perceptible cloak to user-masked key concepts.

sections.heading: Style / copyright.
sections.text: Style mimicry fine-tunes a model on an artist’s works so it can reproduce their signature style on demand, threatening artists’ livelihoods and copyright; a style cloak aims to make the model learn the wrong style from the protected artworks. Glaze [ 131 ] brought cloaking to working artists: its style cloaks make models fine-tuned on the protected artworks learn the wrong artistic style (an end-user tool protecting over 2M images), and it first flagged purification as a threat. Mist [ 77 ] increases transferability with a fused adversarial loss term. Later work diversified whose identity is protected and where the cloak acts: ID-Cloak [ 145 ] learns identity-specific universal cloaks by modeling an identity subspace and optimizing a cloak that transfers across images of the same person, SITA [ 53 ] uses CLIP to decouple and disrupt the style representation of the image when the fine-tuning method is unknown, and StyleProtect [ 144 ] targets selected cross-attention layers.

sections.heading: Editing / inpainting.
sections.text: Text-guided editing takes a real image and a text instruction and returns an altered version of it, while inpainting fills a masked region conditioned on the surrounding content and a prompt; both enable unauthorized manipulation of published photos, so the goal of a cloak here is to derail the edit and leave the output unusable. PhotoGuard [ 127 ] set the template and remains the de-facto baseline: it offers a cheap VAE-encoder attack and a stronger end-to-end diffusion attack that steers generation toward a target image. AdvDM [ 78 ] formulates protection as minimizing the diffusion-model likelihood of a perturbed image, then optimizes a tractable surrogate by maximizing the expected diffusion loss over sampled latent trajectories. SDS [ 174 ] accelerates diffusion-loss attacks via score distillation sampling. EditShield [ 17 ] protects against instruction-guided diffusion editors such as InstructPix2Pix [ 9 ] by adding imperceptible perturbations that shift the instruction-independent conditioning latent, and Anti-Reference [ 139 ] uses a unified weighted loss to jointly target tuning-based customization methods and reference-conditioned generation modules. TarPro [ 132 ] uses a semantic-aware constraint to suppress malicious prompt components while preserving the benign parts of the edit, ACE [ 202 ] makes the attack targeted, steering the predicted score toward one fixed chaotic pattern. FaceLock [ 154 ] erases the subject’s biometric information, AdvI2I [ 189 ] trains a generator whose images drive image-to-image models toward unsafe outputs under benign prompts, and Anti-Diffusion [ 203 ] adds a semantic disturbance loss that drives cross-attention maps toward a zero target. A parallel line hardens cloaks against compression and purification: DCT-Shield [ 5 ] optimizes perturbations over quantized DCT coefficients produced by a JPEG encoding–decoding pipeline, and BlurGuard [ 58 ] adaptively blurs the cloak per semantic region so the protected image better preserves the original image’s power spectrum. As backbones diversified, cloaks followed: PCA [ 37 ] collapses the VAE posterior via KL manipulation, AtkPDM [ 135 ] attacks intermediate U-Net features of pixel-domain models, and DeContext [ 133 ] disrupts the in-context cross-attention flow of DiT editors (FLUX.1 Kontext [ 65 ] ). On the inpainting side, AdvPaint [ 51 ] disrupts self- and cross-attention with separate perturbations inside and outside an enlarged object box, DiffusionGuard [ 21 ] disrupts the early stages of the diffusion process and hardens the cloak via mask augmentation, and introduces InpaintGuardBench, PromptFlare [ 106 ] drives masked-region cross-attention toward the prompt-invariant BOS token, SDA [ 41 ] perturbs first-step self-attention queries to break early contour formation, and Anti-Inpainting [ 36 ] extends protection to unknown masks, prompts, and seeds. Finally, Universal Immunization [ 67 ] amortizes the attack with a single image-agnostic perturbation, and DiffVax [ 113 ] trains a feed-forward immunizer that cloaks unseen images in one pass ( ∼ \sim 250,000 × \times faster), extending to video.

sections.heading: Face-swap / biometric.
sections.text: Face swapping transplants a target identity onto another face, the core mechanism behind deepfakes; cloaks here aim to make swappers extract the wrong identity. FaceSwapGuard [ 156 ] adds imperceptible perturbations that disrupt identity-feature extraction in black-box face-swapping models; My Face Is Mine [ 175 ] uses identity and timestep-averaged deviation losses to craft memory-efficient LDM-latent perturbations that transfer across diffusion-based face swappers; FaceShield [ 52 ] disrupts diffusion face-swappers via source-conditioning attention attacks, facial-feature-extractor attacks, and blur/low-pass noise updates for imperceptibility and JPEG robustness; and AEGIS [ 76 ] injects adversarial signals into the DDIM denoising trajectory, avoiding the pixel-space peak-clipping constraint and disrupting both GAN- and diffusion-based facial manipulation.

sections.heading: 3.1.2 Defenses
sections.text: Here “defense” spans two arenas: (1) purification , Eve’s counters that strip a cloak so her pipeline runs as intended, and (2) unlearning and red-teaming , where a cooperating provider removes or blocks the exploitable capability in the model itself, and red-teamers probe how durable that removal is.

sections.heading: Purification.
sections.text: The direct countermeasure is to preprocess the protected image x + δ x{+}\delta before editing or customization, and even simple lossy transformations strip many cloaks: JPEG compression substantially weakens PhotoGuard -style perturbations [ 128 ] , and black-box Noisy Upscaling [ 47 ] —injecting noise, then reconstructing the image with a generative model—bypasses Glaze , Mist , and Anti-DreamBooth . DiffPure [ 109 ] provides the canonical diffusion-purification formulation, smoothing out adversarial perturbations while preserving image semantics; GrIDPure [ 201 ] adapts it to high-resolution images via small-step purification on overlapping grids with patch averaging; and PDM-Pure [ 173 ] , arguing that perturbations crafted against LDMs transfer poorly to pixel-space diffusion models, purifies with a PDM instead. Since Eve can further modify the customization pipeline itself, many protective perturbations resist neither input-level restoration nor model-level adaptation—motivating newer cloaks that explicitly optimize for survival under purification.

sections.heading: Unlearning and red-teaming.
sections.text: The lightest model-side interventions act at inference: SLD [ 129 ] adds a safety term to classifier-free guidance that steers denoising away from a text-defined unsafe direction without retraining, and GuardT2I [ 180 ] translates guidance embeddings back into natural language to expose intent hidden by adversarial prompts. Training-time erasure instead scrubs the capability from the weights: EraseDiff [ 168 ] redirects forget-set denoising toward mismatched targets for fast unlearning, and Erasing [ 30 ] fine-tunes only the CLIP text encoder on a few images in seconds, though broad concepts resist. GuardDoor [ 190 ] sidesteps the purification arms race by baking a trigger-activated backdoor into the image encoder that survives JPEG, DiffPure , and IMPRESS, at the cost of leaving non-participating editors untouched. Yet automated red-teaming that optimizes adversarial prompts against a guarded model routinely revives “erased” concepts, exposing how shallow such safety can be; AdvUnlearn [ 196 ] responds by adversarially training the CLIP text encoder with utility-preserving regularization, transferring modularly across diffusion backbones, though continuous textual-inversion attacks remain a harder failure mode. Red-teaming also targets the cloaks themselves: DiffShortcut [ 87 ] purifies protected inputs with restoration and super-resolution, then disentangles the personalized concept from residual noise via contrastive decoupling learning, while CAT [ 117 ] trains lightweight LoRA adapters in the LDM autoencoder to realign latent representations distorted by protected samples, without purifying pixels.

sections.heading: 3.2.1 Attacks
sections.text: Video is the fastest-growing surface, contending with the temporal axis and aggressively lossy codecs.

sections.heading: I2V.
sections.text: I2V pipelines (ControlNeXt [ 116 ] , SVD [ 7 ] , CogVideoX [ 182 ] ) animate a reference image, risking misleading content. I2VGuard [ 35 ] , the first white-box I2V defense, composes spatial, temporal, and contrastive-latent losses; UVCG [ 71 ] makes one perturbation universal across videos; Vid-Freeze [ 23 ] freezes motion to the first frame (plausible but static); and Anti-I2V [ 150 ] handles DiT-based I2V via L*a*b* color space / frequency domain-collapse losses, since U-Net cloaks fail on DiTs. DORMANT [ 205 ] extends protection to pose-driven human-image animation, misextracting CLIP and ReferenceNet features with EoT and momentum. Immune2V [ 91 ] , the most principled I2V defense, explains why image cloaks fail on dual-stream I2V (per-frame noise dilutes and text guidance overrides them) and counters with a temporally balanced latent-divergence loss plus alignment to a collapse-inducing trajectory, yielding stronger, more persistent degradation.

sections.heading: Talking-head.
sections.text: Silencer [ 32 ] nullifies audio control (keeping the mouth closed), then aligns DDIM latents for anti-purification; SyncBreaker [ 195 ] attacks the image and audio streams with stage-awareness.

sections.heading: V2V editing.
sections.text: In video-to-video (V2V) editing, PRIME [ 70 ] runs per-frame PhotoGuard with in-loop codec simulation at ∼ 90 % {\sim}90\% lower cost; VideoGuard [ 10 ] then tackles codec non-differentiability directly, optimizing a DDIM latent before gradient-free PSO on pixels; and VGMShield [ 114 ] broadens the scope to lifecycle detection, attribution, and prevention.

sections.heading: T2V safety.
sections.text: T2VAttack [ 69 ] perturbs prompts for semantic/temporal failure and T2V-OptJail [ 84 ] jailbreaks commercial T2V ( ∼ 64 % {\sim}64\% ); in response, T2VShield [ 80 ] rewrites prompts and detects unsafe output ( ∼ 33 % {\sim}33\% ASR drop) and ConceptGuard [ 94 ] flags TI2V risk (ConceptRisk), both evaluated by T2VSafetyBench [ 99 ] .

sections.heading: 3.2.2 Defenses
sections.text: Counter-defenses against video cloaks are still nascent: existing work treats preprocessing and purification as robustness stress tests rather than dedicated removal methods, in contrast to image-domain purification and adaptive counterattacks. IPV-Bench [ 73 ] provides the clearest evidence, evaluating I2V protection under preprocessing attacks and transfer settings and showing that existing protections remain fragile to practical transformations. sections.heading: 3.3.1 Attacks
sections.text: 3D representations are not diffusion models themselves, but they have become an emerging security surface because many 3D assets are now edited through rendered views and diffusion-based guidance.

sections.heading: Editing.
sections.text: DEGauss [ 97 ] protects Gaussian splatting assets by optimizing perturbations over Gaussian representations with view-focal gradient fusion and dual-discrepancy objectives, while AdLift [ 46 ] lifts bounded rendered-view perturbations into safeguard Gaussians so that the protection remains consistent under novel-view interpolation rather than being smoothed away like a naive 2D cloak. Beyond 3DGS editing, Image2Multiview [ 141 ] protects 3D assets by perturbing the source image to disrupt multi-view diffusion and downstream reconstruction.

sections.heading: Poisoning / cost.
sections.text: Recent work also studies broader 3DGS attack surfaces. On the poisoning side, StealthAttack [ 55 ] injects density-guided Gaussian illusions into low-density regions so that malicious objects appear only from selected viewpoints, and GaussTrap [ 45 ] studies stealthy poisoning/backdoor attacks that cause targeted scene confusion while preserving benign views. At the system level, Poison-splat [ 92 ] attacks the computational cost of 3DGS reconstruction. Orthogonal to cloaking, RDSplat [ 199 ] studies watermarking that remains robust under diffusion-based 3DGS editing.

sections.heading: 3.3.2 Defenses
sections.text: Counter-defenses for 3D content remain limited. Existing defenses mainly cover adjacent 3DGS threat models: RemedyGS [ 75 ] uses detect-and-purify mechanisms to protect reconstruction pipelines from poisoned inputs that inflate computation cost, while RDSplat [ 199 ] focuses on provenance rather than cloak removal by embedding watermarks robust to diffusion-based 3DGS editing. These works indicate early system-level and provenance-oriented protections, while general counter-defenses for 3D content cloaks remain open.

sections.heading: 4 Evaluation
sections.text: Evaluation is multi-objective: an attack must be imperceptible , effective , transferable , robust to purification, and efficient , and a defense must satisfy all of these while preserving utility. We briefly consolidate the datasets and benchmarks, target models, and metrics used across the surveyed literature.

In short, image works pair face datasets (CelebA(-HQ) [ 89 ] , VGGFace2 [ 12 ] , FFHQ [ 54 ] ) and art corpora (WikiArt [ 142 ] , ArtBench-10 [ 81 ] ) with general vision corpora (ImageNet [ 126 ] , COCO [ 82 ] ), dedicated editing and inpainting benchmarks (MagicBrush [ 193 ] , EditBench [ 159 ] , InpaintGuardBench [ 21 ] , Defense-Edit [ 203 ] ), and safety prompt sets for guardrails and unlearning (I2P [ 129 ] , MMA-Diffusion [ 179 ] , Ring-A-Bell [ 147 ] , P4D [ 20 ] ). sections.heading: Target models.
sections.text: The Target Models columns of Tables – 3 instantiate Eve’s downstream capability. Image attacks overwhelmingly target the Stable Diffusion family [ 123 ] (v1.x through SDXL), reached through personalization pipelines (DreamBooth [ 125 ] , Textual Inversion [ 31 ] , LoRA variants, Custom Diffusion [ 64 ] ), editors and inpainters (InstructPix2Pix [ 9 ] , SDEdit [ 96 ] , MasaCtrl [ 11 ] , DiffEdit [ 24 ] , SD Inpainting), adapters (T2I-Adapter [ 104 ] , IP-Adapter [ 184 ] ), and, recently, DiT-based editors (FLUX.1 Kontext [ 65 ] ); face-swap cloaks additionally cover diffusion-based swappers (DiffFace [ 60 ] , DiffSwap [ 200 ] , Face-Adapter [ 39 ] ) and GAN-based manipulators (FaceShifter [ 72 ] , SimSwap [ 16 ] , StarGAN [ 22 ] , AttGAN [ 42 ] , HiSD [ 74 ] ), with hosted services (Replicate, NovelAI) probed as black boxes. Video protections target I2V and T2V generators (SVD [ 7 ] , CogVideoX [ 182 ] , DynamiCrafter [ 170 ] , Open-Sora [ 204 ] , I2VGen-XL [ 194 ] , Wan [ 151 ] , HunyuanVideo [ 166 ] ), pose-driven human animators (Animate Anyone [ 48 ] , MagicAnimate [ 172 ] , MagicPose [ 13 ] , Champ [ 206 ] , UniAnimate [ 162 ] ), audio-driven talking heads (Hallo [ 171 ] , EchoMimic [ 19 ] ), zero-shot video editors (TokenFlow [ 33 ] , Text2Video-Zero [ 57 ] , Tune-A-Video [ 167 ] , Fate-Zero [ 121 ] , Video-P2P [ 85 ] , Rerender-A-Video [ 176 ] ), and commercial systems (Pika, Luma, Kling [ 63 ] ). 3D methods attack multi-view diffusion and single-image-to-3D reconstruction (Zero123++ [ 134 ] , Wonder3D [ 90 ] ), instruction-guided 3DGS/NeRF editors (GaussianEditor [ 155 ] , DGE [ 15 ] , DreamCatalyst [ 59 ] , EditSplat [ 68 ] , Instruct-GS2GS [ 148 ] ), and reconstruction backbones (3DGS [ 56 ] , Scaffold-GS [ 93 ] , Instant-NGP [ 105 ] ).

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: We group the reported metrics into six recurring categories; the middle four correspond to the IA, FA, TR, and RB columns of Tables – 3 , while effectiveness and efficiency are reported by virtually every work. Table 5 formalizes the individual metrics—their inputs, outputs, what they measure, and the direction indicating successful protection. Effectiveness compares generations from protected inputs against those from clean inputs: FID, LPIPS, SSIM/PSNR, and CLIP similarity for images, complemented by FDFR and ISM in face-centric pipelines; optical-flow similarity, frame consistency, lip-sync scores, and attack-success rate for video; and held-out novel-view fidelity with cross-view consistency for 3D. Imperceptibility (IA) instead compares the protected input against its clean source (PSNR, LPIPS, MS-SSIM, and human or VLM studies). Failure analysis (FA) probes where a protection breaks down (atypical content; unseen prompts, masks, or seeds); it has no standardized metric and remains the least consistently reported dimension. Transferability (TR) re-measures effectiveness on backbones, samplers, and tasks the cloak was not optimized against, most notably across the U-Net-to-DiT shift. Robustness (RB) re-runs the effectiveness protocol after purification (JPEG compression, cropping, additive noise, DiffPure [ 109 ] , PDM-Pure [ 173 ] ), instantiating the minimax of Equation ( 4 ). Finally, efficiency reports protection cost per asset, separating per-sample optimizers from amortized generators that are orders of magnitude faster [ 1 , 113 ] . sections.heading: 5 Open Challenges and Conclusion
sections.text: Despite rapid progress, the adversarial robustness of diffusion models remains an open problem. We distill the primary challenges cutting across image, video, and 3D into three high-leverage directions for future work.

sections.heading: Adaptive countermeasures and evaluation.
sections.text: Most protective cloaks are vulnerable to a continuous cycle of neutralization by model-side preprocessing or input purification. Because the party deploying the model controls the input pipeline, fixed perturbations are routinely mitigated by adaptive transformations, such as lossy compression, adaptive blurring, or diffusion-based regeneration. Breaking this cycle requires moving away from empirical hardening against known countermeasures toward certified defenses that hold against broad classes of unseen purifiers. Furthermore, progress is obscured by a lack of standardized benchmarks. Evaluating against static baselines frequently overstates real-world protection; robust evaluation must integrate common datasets, threat models, and adaptive purifier suites to ensure apparent progress can be trusted.

sections.heading: Cross-model and cross-sample generalization.
sections.text: Current immunizers typically rely on test-time optimization tailored to a specific white-box backbone and a single asset. This process is computationally expensive and transfers poorly to real-world commercial services, where model weights, architectures, and preprocessing steps are completely hidden behind black-box APIs. To be practical, cloaks must attack components shared across multiple pipelines. Simultaneously, future work must resolve the tension between per-sample strength and cross-sample speed. Developing universal perturbations or amortized generators capable of protecting arbitrary unseen content in a single forward pass—without sacrificing the robustness of bespoke optimization—remains a critical open problem.

sections.heading: Theoretical foundations and modality expansion.
sections.text: While research is heavily concentrated on the image domain, extending protection to video and 3D assets—arguably the higher-stakes settings for real-world misuse, such as deepfakes—remains an urgent frontier. These advanced modalities introduce complex structural constraints: video adds a temporal axis that dilutes per-frame cloaks alongside aggressive compression codecs, while 3D requires perturbations that survive multi-view rendering pipelines without being smoothed away. Overcoming these challenges requires transitioning from empirical trial-and-error to a principled, theoretical characterization of the adversarial perturbation space. A systematic mapping of which geometric and semantic directions fundamentally survive purification and multi-modal transformations would turn the current empirical patchwork into a predictive science.

sections.heading: Conclusion.
sections.text: We surveyed adversarial attacks and defenses for diffusion models across image, video, and 3D under a unified, task-centric framework. The literature demonstrates that static, single-target protections are no longer sufficient in an environment of adaptive countermeasures. Sustained progress in content immunization now depends on developing defenses that generalize across diverse models and samples, establishing standardized adaptive evaluation metrics, and scaling robust protective frameworks to under-studied video and 3D domains.

However, their widespread public availability enables misuse at scale, motivating a rapidly growing body of research on adversarial attacks and defenses. This survey provides, to our knowledge, the first unified review of this literature across three visual modalities: image, video, and 3D. We introduce a comprehensive, task-centric taxonomy: we first divide the literature by modality; within each modality, we separate methods into attacks and defenses, and then group them by the generative task they target, presenting them chronologically within each task. Moreover, we provide an in-depth analysis of their evaluation settings, consolidating the datasets, metrics, and benchmarks used to assess them. We conclude by identifying several open challenges and outlining concrete future research directions. Project Webpage : https://github.com/ozgurkara99/awesome-adv-attack-defense-on-diffusion . Keywords: Diffusion models ⋅ \cdot Adversarial attacks ⋅ \cdot Adversarial defenses 1 Introduction Diffusion models (DMs) [ 44 , 138 , 123 ] have surpassed GANs [ 34 , 122 , 4 , 54 , 103 ] to become the dominant family of deep generative models, expanding from high-fidelity image synthesis [ 28 , 123 ] to video [ 137 , 43 , 182 , 116 , 95 ] and 3D content generation [ 120 , 169 , 185 , 207 , 155 ] , while their architectures evolved from U-Nets [ 124 ] to diffusion transformers (DiTs) [ 115 ] . Now publicly available as open-source releases and commercial services [ 123 , 100 , 111 , 112 , 63 ] , DMs place unprecedented generative power in anyone’s hands, making misuse a threat at scale. Because each modality supports its own generative tasks, every task opens a distinct attack surface: images face unauthorized personalization, style transfer, and face swapping; videos, manipulated talking-head animations and deepfake editing; and 3D assets, instruction-driven scene alterations. These harms were first met reactively , through deepfake detection and watermark-based authentication, but such post-hoc measures are easily circumvented, and the field has since turned proactive , aiming to make content inherently resistant to exploitation before it is misused. This shift defines the literature we survey: adversarial attacks and defenses for diffusion models . {forest} Figure 1 : Organization of this survey. After motivating the problem (§ 1 ) and establishing background and a unified adversarial framework (§ 2 ), we review attacks and defenses by their target modality (§ 3 ), consolidate their evaluation settings (§ 4 ), and conclude by outlining high-leverage directions for future research (§ 5 ). Adversarial attacks and defenses for DMs differ fundamentally from their counterparts on classification models, introducing novel challenges. (1) Task and setting heterogeneity : Whereas a classifier presents a single, well-defined decision boundary, generative pipelines vary widely in task, input modality, and backbone architecture, so protections crafted for one setting transfer poorly to another. (2) Multi-step, conditional, and stochastic generation : Instead of fooling one deterministic forward pass, a perturbation must remain effective across an iterative denoising trajectory with random noise draws and user-chosen conditioning, and optimizing through this long chain is far more expensive than a one-step attack. (3) An adaptive adversary : Uniquely, the party deploying the model often acts as the adversary; it controls the entire pipeline and can preprocess inputs or modify the model itself to strip or circumvent protections, so protections must hold against a moving target rather than a fixed one. This literature has grown quickly but remains fragmented, and no existing survey covers all visual modalities. Table positions our work against nine related surveys. Notably, none address 3D content, making ours the first to jointly cover image, video, and 3D with a primary focus on adversarial robustness. Existing general adversarial-robustness surveys for DMs remain exclusively image-centric [ 192 , 118 , 146 , 191 , 165 , 2 ] . The surveys that do reach video approach it strictly through facial deepfakes and the detection or disruption of AI-generated media [ 108 , 26 ] . The remaining survey studies replication, trustworthiness, copyright, and watermarking, where adversarial robustness is at most peripheral [ 161 ] . Beyond coverage, the deeper problem is organization. Prior taxonomies sort methods by perturbation space or threat category—axes that describe how a method operates, but not what it protects against—leaving works that target the same misuse scattered and incomparable. In practice, both misuse and protection are task-specific: a diffusion model is attacked through a concrete generative task, and each modality imposes its own structural constraints—precisely why methods transfer poorly across tasks, modalities, and backbones. We therefore organize the literature first by modality, then into attacks and defenses, and finally by the generative task they target, ordered chronologically within each task. This makes methods addressing the same threat directly comparable, exposes each task’s attack/counterattack arms race, and localizes modality-specific challenges where they belong. Figure 1 summarizes the resulting organization. To summarize, we provide (i) the first unified review of adversarial attacks and defenses for DMs covering all visual domains, namely image, video and 3D, under a single immunization framework (Section 2.2 ); (ii) a task-centric taxonomy that categorizes methods first by modality and then by the generative task they attack or protect (Figure 3 ), making methods that target the same task directly comparable; (iii) a consolidated treatment of the datasets, metrics, dedicated benchmarks, and analyses used to evaluate them (Section 4 ; Tables , 2 , 3 ); and (iv) an outline of open challenges with concrete future research directions (Section 5 ). 2 Preliminaries This section provides the necessary background: Section 2.1 reviews diffusion modeling, dominant architectures, and modality-specific attack surfaces. Section 2.2 then formalizes a unified adversarial framework spanning both attacks and defenses. 2.1 Background on Diffusion Models Diffusion modeling. Diffusion models generate data by learning to invert a gradual, stochastic corruption process. In denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) [ 44 , 138 ] , a forward process progressively adds Gaussian noise to a clean sample 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} , yielding 𝐱 t = α ¯ t ​ 𝐱 0 + 1 − α ¯ t ​ ϵ \mathbf{x}_{t}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon} . A neural network ϵ θ \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta} is trained to reverse this process by predicting the injected noise at each timestep t t : L simple = 𝔼 t , 𝐱 0 , ϵ ​ [ ‖ ϵ − ϵ θ ​ ( α ¯ t ​ 𝐱 0 + 1 − α ¯ t ​ ϵ , t ) ‖ 2 ] . L_{\mathrm{simple}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,\mathbf{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}\!\left[\|\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\theta}(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\mathbf{x}_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon},\,t)\|^{2}\right]. (1) Generation iteratively applies this learned denoiser to pure noise. By conditioning the reverse process on auxiliary inputs, DMs offer a versatile generative framework. Equation ( 1 ) is the core learning objective and identically the target most adversarial cloaks seek to maximize: a sample the model cannot accurately denoise is one it can neither learn from nor faithfully manipulate, effectively paralyzing the generative pipeline. Model architectures. The denoiser’s architecture dictates how information is processed and subsequently attacked. U-Net-based [ 7 , 123 ] models rely on a convolutional encoder-decoder, injecting conditioning signals through localized cross-attention layers. Adversaries typically exploit this by targeting specific convolutional features or disrupting cross-attention maps. Conversely, DiT-based models [ 115 ] —powering modern state-of-the-art pipelines [ 182 , 112 , 151 , 38 , 65 ] —replace the U-Net with a transformer backbone. DiTs operate on flattened patches, merging spatial, temporal, and conditioning tokens into a single self-attention sequence. This shift invalidates many U-Net cloaks, as global self-attention scatters a perturbation’s localized impact, requiring attackers to design architecture-aware perturbations tailored specifically to DiT token-mixing. Modalities. DMs permeate the three vision domains surveyed in this work, each introducing distinct vulnerabilities. Images are the native setting; a single backbone supports numerous tasks, making it the most heavily studied attack surface. Video DMs extend image backbones with temporal attention or spatio-temporal patches [ 7 , 171 , 182 ] . This complicates protection: per-frame cloaks dilute over time, cross-frame attention mixes features, and aggressive compression codecs strip non-robust perturbations. Finally, 3D representations [ 102 , 157 , 56 ] are not DMs themselves, but modern 3D pipelines rely on 2D DMs as priors or guidance. Adversarial methods here must account for multi-view consistency, defining budgets over rendered views or directly within the 3D parameters. Figure 2 : Diffusion-model immunization across modalities. Because a single backbone supports numerous downstream tasks, each acts as a unique attack surface. We categorize these methods below by their targeted generative task, structured chronologically within Table . Personalization. Personalization methods fine-tune a diffusion model on a few images of a subject so it can regenerate that subject in new contexts; misused, they enable identity theft and non-consensual imagery, so the goal of a cloak here is to make fine-tuning on the protected images fail. Anti-DreamBooth [ 149 ] set the template and remains the baseline: it optimizes δ \delta to corrupt the DreamBooth personalization loop itself, instantiating the bilevel objective of ( 2 ). SimAC [ 153 ] makes anti-customization stronger by attacking the useful timesteps and features, InMark [ 83 ] embeds protective watermarks on influential pixels, using influence-function-inspired pixel selection so that personalized fine-tuning fails even after common image modifications, MetaCloak [ 88 ] learns transferable, robust perturbations via meta-learning, transfers cloak to a commercial service (Replicate), DisDiff [ 86 ] erases subject-token attention to break the text-subject binding, and DADiff [ 143 ] combines prompt-level and image-level adversarial attacks to disrupt customization more thoroughly. A later line hardens the cloak against purification: HF-Anti-DreamBooth [ 110 ] concentrates perturbation power in high-frequency regions of the image that low-pass purifiers miss, AntiPure [ 178 ] constructs perturbations that persist through diffusion-based purification, and LDU [ 27 ] shifts the denoising trajectory of diffusion models. FastProtect [ 1 ] reduces cost by replacing per-image optimization with a pre-trained perturbation generator (200–3500 × \times faster). IDDM [ 25 ] protects personalized generation while disrupting face recognition of the generated images. VCPro [ 98 ] confines the least-perceptible cloak to user-masked key concepts. Style / copyright. Style mimicry fine-tunes a model on an artist’s works so it can reproduce their signature style on demand, threatening artists’ livelihoods and copyright; a style cloak aims to make the model learn the wrong style from the protected artworks. Glaze [ 131 ] brought cloaking to working artists: its style cloaks make models fine-tuned on the protected artworks learn the wrong artistic style (an end-user tool protecting over 2M images), and it first flagged purification as a threat. Mist [ 77 ] increases transferability with a fused adversarial loss term. Later work diversified whose identity is protected and where the cloak acts: ID-Cloak [ 145 ] learns identity-specific universal cloaks by modeling an identity subspace and optimizing a cloak that transfers across images of the same person, SITA [ 53 ] uses CLIP to decouple and disrupt the style representation of the image when the fine-tuning method is unknown, and StyleProtect [ 144 ] targets selected cross-attention layers. Editing / inpainting. Text-guided editing takes a real image and a text instruction and returns an altered version of it, while inpainting fills a masked region conditioned on the surrounding content and a prompt; both enable unauthorized manipulation of published photos, so the goal of a cloak here is to derail the edit and leave the output unusable. PhotoGuard [ 127 ] set the template and remains the de-facto baseline: it offers a cheap VAE-encoder attack and a stronger end-to-end diffusion attack that steers generation toward a target image. AdvDM [ 78 ] formulates protection as minimizing the diffusion-model likelihood of a perturbed image, then optimizes a tractable surrogate by maximizing the expected diffusion loss over sampled latent trajectories. SDS [ 174 ] accelerates diffusion-loss attacks via score distillation sampling. EditShield [ 17 ] protects against instruction-guided diffusion editors such as InstructPix2Pix [ 9 ] by adding imperceptible perturbations that shift the instruction-independent conditioning latent, and Anti-Reference [ 139 ] uses a unified weighted loss to jointly target tuning-based customization methods and reference-conditioned generation modules. TarPro [ 132 ] uses a semantic-aware constraint to suppress malicious prompt components while preserving the benign parts of the edit, ACE [ 202 ] makes the attack targeted, steering the predicted score toward one fixed chaotic pattern. FaceLock [ 154 ] erases the subject’s biometric information, AdvI2I [ 189 ] trains a generator whose images drive image-to-image models toward unsafe outputs under benign prompts, and Anti-Diffusion [ 203 ] adds a semantic disturbance loss that drives cross-attention maps toward a zero target. A parallel line hardens cloaks against compression and purification: DCT-Shield [ 5 ] optimizes perturbations over quantized DCT coefficients produced by a JPEG encoding–decoding pipeline, and BlurGuard [ 58 ] adaptively blurs the cloak per semantic region so the protected image better preserves the original image’s power spectrum. As backbones diversified, cloaks followed: PCA [ 37 ] collapses the VAE posterior via KL manipulation, AtkPDM [ 135 ] attacks intermediate U-Net features of pixel-domain models, and DeContext [ 133 ] disrupts the in-context cross-attention flow of DiT editors (FLUX.1 Kontext [ 65 ] ). On the inpainting side, AdvPaint [ 51 ] disrupts self- and cross-attention with separate perturbations inside and outside an enlarged object box, DiffusionGuard [ 21 ] disrupts the early stages of the diffusion process and hardens the cloak via mask augmentation, and introduces InpaintGuardBench, PromptFlare [ 106 ] drives masked-region cross-attention toward the prompt-invariant BOS token, SDA [ 41 ] perturbs first-step self-attention queries to break early contour formation, and Anti-Inpainting [ 36 ] extends protection to unknown masks, prompts, and seeds. Finally, Universal Immunization [ 67 ] amortizes the attack with a single image-agnostic perturbation, and DiffVax [ 113 ] trains a feed-forward immunizer that cloaks unseen images in one pass ( ∼ \sim 250,000 × \times faster), extending to video. Face-swap / biometric. Face swapping transplants a target identity onto another face, the core mechanism behind deepfakes; cloaks here aim to make swappers extract the wrong identity. FaceSwapGuard [ 156 ] adds imperceptible perturbations that disrupt identity-feature extraction in black-box face-swapping models; My Face Is Mine [ 175 ] uses identity and timestep-averaged deviation losses to craft memory-efficient LDM-latent perturbations that transfer across diffusion-based face swappers; FaceShield [ 52 ] disrupts diffusion face-swappers via source-conditioning attention attacks, facial-feature-extractor attacks, and blur/low-pass noise updates for imperceptibility and JPEG robustness; and AEGIS [ 76 ] injects adversarial signals into the DDIM denoising trajectory, avoiding the pixel-space peak-clipping constraint and disrupting both GAN- and diffusion-based facial manipulation. 3.1.2 Defenses Here “defense” spans two arenas: (1) purification , Eve’s counters that strip a cloak so her pipeline runs as intended, and (2) unlearning and red-teaming , where a cooperating provider removes or blocks the exploitable capability in the model itself, and red-teamers probe how durable that removal is. Purification. The direct countermeasure is to preprocess the protected image x + δ x{+}\delta before editing or customization, and even simple lossy transformations strip many cloaks: JPEG compression substantially weakens PhotoGuard -style perturbations [ 128 ] , and black-box Noisy Upscaling [ 47 ] —injecting noise, then reconstructing the image with a generative model—bypasses Glaze , Mist , and Anti-DreamBooth . DiffPure [ 109 ] provides the canonical diffusion-purification formulation, smoothing out adversarial perturbations while preserving image semantics; GrIDPure [ 201 ] adapts it to high-resolution images via small-step purification on overlapping grids with patch averaging; and PDM-Pure [ 173 ] , arguing that perturbations crafted against LDMs transfer poorly to pixel-space diffusion models, purifies with a PDM instead. Since Eve can further modify the customization pipeline itself, many protective perturbations resist neither input-level restoration nor model-level adaptation—motivating newer cloaks that explicitly optimize for survival under purification. Unlearning and red-teaming. The lightest model-side interventions act at inference: SLD [ 129 ] adds a safety term to classifier-free guidance that steers denoising away from a text-defined unsafe direction without retraining, and GuardT2I [ 180 ] translates guidance embeddings back into natural language to expose intent hidden by adversarial prompts. Training-time erasure instead scrubs the capability from the weights: EraseDiff [ 168 ] redirects forget-set denoising toward mismatched targets for fast unlearning, and Erasing [ 30 ] fine-tunes only the CLIP text encoder on a few images in seconds, though broad concepts resist. GuardDoor [ 190 ] sidesteps the purification arms race by baking a trigger-activated backdoor into the image encoder that survives JPEG, DiffPure , and IMPRESS, at the cost of leaving non-participating editors untouched. Yet automated red-teaming that optimizes adversarial prompts against a guarded model routinely revives “erased” concepts, exposing how shallow such safety can be; AdvUnlearn [ 196 ] responds by adversarially training the CLIP text encoder with utility-preserving regularization, transferring modularly across diffusion backbones, though continuous textual-inversion attacks remain a harder failure mode. Red-teaming also targets the cloaks themselves: DiffShortcut [ 87 ] purifies protected inputs with restoration and super-resolution, then disentangles the personalized concept from residual noise via contrastive decoupling learning, while CAT [ 117 ] trains lightweight LoRA adapters in the LDM autoencoder to realign latent representations distorted by protected samples, without purifying pixels. 3.2 Video Table 2 : Video attack and defense methods. I2V. I2V pipelines (ControlNeXt [ 116 ] , SVD [ 7 ] , CogVideoX [ 182 ] ) animate a reference image, risking misleading content. I2VGuard [ 35 ] , the first white-box I2V defense, composes spatial, temporal, and contrastive-latent losses; UVCG [ 71 ] makes one perturbation universal across videos; Vid-Freeze [ 23 ] freezes motion to the first frame (plausible but static); and Anti-I2V [ 150 ] handles DiT-based I2V via L*a*b* color space / frequency domain-collapse losses, since U-Net cloaks fail on DiTs. DORMANT [ 205 ] extends protection to pose-driven human-image animation, misextracting CLIP and ReferenceNet features with EoT and momentum. Immune2V [ 91 ] , the most principled I2V defense, explains why image cloaks fail on dual-stream I2V (per-frame noise dilutes and text guidance overrides them) and counters with a temporally balanced latent-divergence loss plus alignment to a collapse-inducing trajectory, yielding stronger, more persistent degradation. Talking-head. Silencer [ 32 ] nullifies audio control (keeping the mouth closed), then aligns DDIM latents for anti-purification; SyncBreaker [ 195 ] attacks the image and audio streams with stage-awareness. V2V editing. Editing. DEGauss [ 97 ] protects Gaussian splatting assets by optimizing perturbations over Gaussian representations with view-focal gradient fusion and dual-discrepancy objectives, while AdLift [ 46 ] lifts bounded rendered-view perturbations into safeguard Gaussians so that the protection remains consistent under novel-view interpolation rather than being smoothed away like a naive 2D cloak. Beyond 3DGS editing, Image2Multiview [ 141 ] protects 3D assets by perturbing the source image to disrupt multi-view diffusion and downstream reconstruction. Poisoning / cost. Recent work also studies broader 3DGS attack surfaces. On the poisoning side, StealthAttack [ 55 ] injects density-guided Gaussian illusions into low-density regions so that malicious objects appear only from selected viewpoints, and GaussTrap [ 45 ] studies stealthy poisoning/backdoor attacks that cause targeted scene confusion while preserving benign views. At the system level, Poison-splat [ 92 ] attacks the computational cost of 3DGS reconstruction. Orthogonal to cloaking, RDSplat [ 199 ] studies watermarking that remains robust under diffusion-based 3DGS editing. 3.3.2 Defenses Counter-defenses for 3D content remain limited. Existing defenses mainly cover adjacent 3DGS threat models: RemedyGS [ 75 ] uses detect-and-purify mechanisms to protect reconstruction pipelines from poisoned inputs that inflate computation cost, while RDSplat [ 199 ] focuses on provenance rather than cloak removal by embedding watermarks robust to diffusion-based 3DGS editing. These works indicate early system-level and provenance-oriented protections, while general counter-defenses for 3D content cloaks remain open. 4 Evaluation Evaluation is multi-objective: an attack must be imperceptible , effective , transferable , robust to purification, and efficient , and a defense must satisfy all of these while preserving utility.
